Is this job offer real? How to spot a fake job in Kenya

Fake job offers target young people who are searching hard and hoping. That is not your fault — and there are clear warning signs that expose almost every scam. Learn them once, and you’ll see them everywhere.

The golden rule: a real job never asks you to pay. Ever.

Eight warning signs

1

They ask you to pay

Registration fee, training fee, medical fee, uniform fee, “refundable” deposit — it doesn’t matter what they call it. A real employer pays you, not the other way round.

2

The pay is too good for the work

Entry-level “typing job” paying KES 150,000 a month? Salaries far above the market for easy work are bait, not luck.

3

They offer you the job instantly

No interview, no questions about your skills, hired within minutes of applying. Real hiring takes at least one real conversation.

4

Everything happens on WhatsApp only

A real company has a real footprint: a website, an office, a registered name you can search. An offer that exists only inside a chat thread usually isn’t real.

5

The job description is vague

“Online work, flexible hours, weekly pay” — but they can’t say what you’ll actually do, for whom, or how the pay is calculated. Vagueness hides the trap.

6

They pressure you to decide now

“Only 3 slots left, confirm within the hour.” Urgency is manufactured so you don’t stop to think or ask anyone.

7

They ask for your PIN, OTP or documents upfront

No employer needs your M-Pesa PIN, bank OTP or original documents before you’ve even interviewed. That’s identity theft, not recruitment.

8

The email or profile doesn’t match the company

A “manager” at a big company writing from a free Gmail address, a logo that looks slightly off, a website registered last month. Check the details — scammers rarely get them all right.

If you spot one, do this

1

Do not pay, and do not share your PIN, OTP, or documents.

2

Stop replying. You don’t owe a scammer a goodbye message.

3

Report it — through Inuka’s Report a concern channel if you saw it in the program, or to Safaricom (report to 333) and the DCI if money was taken.

4

Warn a friend. Scams spread through trust networks — so should warnings.

How Inuka protects you

Every role shared through Inuka is reviewed by Fuzu before you see it: real employer, clear pay, safe conditions, no fees. Employers also sign the Fair Work Pledge — a public commitment to fair treatment, pay transparency and a strict no-fee policy.
